blocks.text: A relation is the mathematical idea of "these two things are connected," made precise. Once sets exist, the very next natural question is how elements of one set relate to elements of another, or to each other within the same set. A relation answers that question directly: it is simply a set of ordered pairs, each pair recording one connection. From this one small definition comes an enormous amount of structure, including the equality relation, the less than or equal to ordering on numbers, and, closer to AI engineering, the structure behind every database join and every user-item interaction table that powers a recommender system.

blocks.alt: A relation as a set of ordered pairs between two sets
blocks.caption: Relations carry properties like reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, and can be drawn as a matrix or graph

1. What a Relation Is

A relation from a set A to a set B is a set of ordered pairs, where the first element of each pair comes from A and the second comes from B. If a pair (a, b) is in the relation R, this is written a R b, read as "a relates to b," and it means precisely that the connection R holds between a and b, nothing more and nothing less than what is explicitly listed in the set of pairs.

A relation does not need a formula or a rule; any set of ordered pairs drawn from A and B qualifies as a relation, even one that looks arbitrary. In practice, most useful relations are defined by a rule, such as "a is less than b" or "user a purchased product b," because a rule is a compact way to describe what would otherwise be an enormous, possibly infinite, list of pairs.

code.content:
# A relation as an explicit set of ordered pairs
likes = {("alice", "jazz"), ("alice", "rock"), ("bob", "jazz")}

print(("alice", "jazz") in likes)  # True: alice relates to jazz
print(("bob", "rock") in likes)    # False: no such pair recorded

blocks.text: 2. The Cartesian Product

Before defining a relation formally, it helps to name the set every possible pair could be drawn from. The Cartesian product of A and B, written A times B, is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a is an element of A and b is an element of B. A relation from A to B is then, by definition, simply a subset of A times B: it does not have to include every possible pair, only the ones for which the connection actually holds.

The size of the Cartesian product is the product of the two set sizes: if A has 3 elements and B has 4 elements, A times B has 12 ordered pairs in total. This immediately tells you the largest a relation between A and B could possibly be, and it is the space that any specific relation is carved out of.
3. Domain and Range

The domain of a relation R is the set of all first elements that appear in some pair of R, and the range is the set of all second elements that appear in some pair. Neither has to equal the full sets A or B the relation was drawn from; an element of A that never appears as a first coordinate in any pair of R simply does not participate in the relation at all.

This distinction matters in practice: a user-purchase relation drawn from all registered users and all catalog products will typically have a domain much smaller than the full user set, since not every registered user has made a purchase, and a range smaller than the full catalog, since not every product has ever been bought.
4. Reflexive Relations

A relation R on a set A is reflexive if every element of A relates to itself, that is, (a, a) is in R for every a in A. Reflexivity is a statement about the whole set: it fails the moment even a single element of A does not relate to itself, regardless of how many other pairs are present.

Equality is the cleanest example of a reflexive relation, since every element equals itself. "Is a friend of" on a social network is typically not reflexive, since a person is not usually listed as their own friend, while "lives in the same city as" is reflexive, since everyone trivially lives in the same city as themselves.
5. Symmetric Relations

A relation R on a set A is symmetric if whenever (a, b) is in R, the reverse pair (b, a) is also in R. Symmetry means direction does not matter: the relation is a statement about an unordered connection between a and b, even though it is still technically stored as ordered pairs.

"Is married to" is symmetric, since if a is married to b, then b is married to a. "Follows on a social network" is typically not symmetric, since a can follow b without b following a back, which is precisely why platforms distinguish "followers" from "friends," the latter usually requiring the symmetric, mutual version of the relation.
6. Transitive Relations

A relation R on a set A is transitive if whenever (a, b) is in R and (b, c) is in R, the pair (a, c) is also in R. Transitivity is what lets a relation chain through an intermediate element: it guarantees that connections compose, so a direct link from a to c is forced to exist whenever an indirect two-step path through b exists.

"Is an ancestor of" is transitive: if a is an ancestor of b, and b is an ancestor of c, then a is an ancestor of c. "Is a friend of" is famously not transitive in real social networks: a being friends with b, and b being friends with c, does not force a and c to be friends, which is exactly why friend-of-a-friend recommendation features exist, to surface connections the raw relation does not already contain.

blocks.title: Why this matters for recommendations
blocks.content: A friend-of-a-friend suggestion algorithm is directly exploiting the fact that friendship is not transitive; if it were, there would be no new people left to suggest, since everyone reachable in two steps would already be a direct friend.

blocks.text: 7. Equivalence Relations

A relation that is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric, and transitive is called an equivalence relation. This combination of the three properties is special enough to have its own name because it captures precisely the idea of "these elements are interchangeable for some purpose," which is exactly what the word equivalence suggests.

The most familiar equivalence relation is ordinary equality: every number equals itself (reflexive), if a equals b then b equals a (symmetric), and if a equals b and b equals c then a equals c (transitive). Another common example is "has the same remainder when divided by n," which groups integers into n buckets based purely on remainder, regardless of how different the numbers themselves look.
7.1 Checking All Three Properties Together

Verifying that a relation is an equivalence relation requires checking all three properties independently; a relation can satisfy any two of the three while failing the third, and it takes all three together to earn the name. "Lives in the same city as" is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation, while "is friends with" typically fails both symmetry, in the directed-follow sense, and transitivity, so it does not qualify.
8. Equivalence Classes

Once a relation is confirmed to be an equivalence relation, it automatically partitions its underlying set into disjoint groups called equivalence classes, where every element in a group is related to every other element in that same group, and to no element outside it. Each equivalence class can be represented by any one of its members, since all members are, by definition, interchangeable under the relation.

For "has the same remainder when divided by 3" over the integers, the equivalence classes are exactly three buckets: the numbers with remainder 0, the numbers with remainder 1, and the numbers with remainder 2. Every integer falls into exactly one of these three classes, and this partitioning property, splitting a set into clean, non-overlapping groups, is what makes equivalence relations so useful for tasks like clustering near-duplicate records.

code.content:
from collections import defaultdict

numbers = range(10)
classes = defaultdict(list)
for n in numbers:
    classes[n % 3].append(n)

for remainder, members in classes.items():
    print(f"remainder {remainder}: {members}")
# remainder 0: [0, 3, 6, 9]
# remainder 1: [1, 4, 7]
# remainder 2: [2, 5, 8]

blocks.text: 9. Representing a Relation as a Matrix

A relation on a finite set A can be represented as a square matrix, with one row and one column for every element of A. The entry in row a, column b is 1 if (a, b) is in the relation, and 0 otherwise. This is called the adjacency matrix of the relation, a term borrowed directly from graph theory, since a relation and a graph are, as the next section shows, really the same object viewed two ways.

The matrix view makes several properties easy to read off visually: a reflexive relation has every diagonal entry equal to 1, a symmetric relation has a matrix that is a mirror image of itself across the diagonal, and the total number of 1 entries equals the number of pairs in the relation.

code.content:
import numpy as np

elements = ["a", "b", "c"]
index = {e: i for i, e in enumerate(elements)}
relation = {("a", "a"), ("a", "b"), ("b", "b"), ("c", "a"), ("c", "c")}

matrix = np.zeros((len(elements), len(elements)), dtype=int)
for (x, y) in relation:
    matrix[index[x], index[y]] = 1

print(matrix)
# [[1 1 0]
#  [0 1 0]
#  [1 0 1]]

blocks.text: 10. Representing a Relation as a Directed Graph

A relation on a set A can equally be drawn as a directed graph: each element of A becomes a node, or vertex, and each pair (a, b) in the relation becomes a directed edge, or arrow, pointing from a to b. This is precisely the same information as the matrix from the previous section, drawn as a picture instead of a grid of numbers; a full treatment of vertices, edges, and graph terminology is the subject of the graph theory basics lesson that follows this one.

The graph view makes some properties even easier to see than the matrix does: reflexivity shows up as a small loop at every node, symmetry shows up as every arrow having a matching arrow pointing back the opposite way, and transitivity shows up as every two-step path having a direct shortcut edge already drawn in.

blocks.text: 11. Partial Orders, Briefly

A relation that is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric, meaning that (a, b) and (b, a) both being in the relation forces a to equal b, is called a partial order. The less than or equal to relation on numbers is the standard example: it is reflexive, since every number is less than or equal to itself, transitive, and antisymmetric, since a being less than or equal to b and b being less than or equal to a can only happen if a equals b.

Partial orders differ from equivalence relations in a key way: instead of grouping elements together as interchangeable, they rank elements against each other, though not necessarily every pair needs to be comparable, which is why it is called a partial, rather than total, order. The subset relation from the sets lesson is another partial order: A subset of B and B subset of A together force A to equal B, matching the antisymmetric requirement exactly.
12. AI Relevance: Database Joins

A relational database table is, quite literally, a relation in the mathematical sense: a set of rows, each row an ordered tuple of values, drawn from the Cartesian product of each columns possible values. A join operation between two tables is the database engineerings direct analogue of composing relations, matching rows where a shared key relates an entry in one table to an entry in another.

An inner join between a users table and an orders table produces exactly the set of pairs (user, order) where the user id relation actually holds, discarding users with no orders and orders with no matching user, precisely mirroring how the domain of a mathematical relation only contains elements that actually participate in at least one pair.
13. AI Relevance: Recommendation Systems and Similarity Relations

A recommendation system is built on top of a user-item relation: a set of ordered pairs (user, item) recording every interaction, such as a purchase, a click, or a rating above some threshold. This relation is typically neither symmetric, since a user interacting with an item does not mean the item interacts back, nor transitive on its own, which is exactly why collaborative filtering algorithms exist, to infer new, plausible pairs that are not directly present in the observed relation.

Similarity relations are a second, equally important use of this idea: define a relation "is similar to" between items based on shared purchasers, or between users based on overlapping purchase history, then use that relation, which is usually built to be symmetric by construction, as the backbone of a "customers who bought this also bought" feature. Whether such a similarity relation is treated as reflexive, symmetric, or an approximate equivalence relation directly shapes how the recommendation algorithm behaves.

blocks.text: 13.1 Why the Relation Is Usually Sparse

In practice the user-item relation is extremely sparse: out of every possible (user, item) pair in the full Cartesian product, only a tiny fraction actually appear, since a typical user interacts with a vanishingly small slice of a large catalog. This sparsity is precisely why recommendation systems cannot simply look up an existing relation and instead must predict which currently-missing pairs are likely to become true relation entries in the future.
14. Worked Example

Consider the relation R on the set A equals 1, 2, 3, 4 defined by "a R b if and only if a and b have the same remainder when divided by 2," meaning both are even or both are odd. Determine whether R is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, then list its equivalence classes if it qualifies as an equivalence relation.

code.content:
A = {1, 2, 3, 4}
R = {(a, b) for a in A for b in A if a % 2 == b % 2}
print(sorted(R))
# [(1, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2), (2, 4), (3, 1), (3, 3), (4, 2), (4, 4)]

print(is_reflexive(R, A))    # True: every element matches its own parity
print(is_symmetric(R))       # True: parity matching is order independent
print(is_transitive(R))      # True: matching parities chain through any middle element

blocks.text: Since R is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, it is an equivalence relation, and it partitions A into exactly two equivalence classes: the odd numbers, 1 and 3, and the even numbers, 2 and 4. Every element of one class relates to every other element of the same class, and to no element of the other class, exactly matching the definition from section 8.

Notice that checking all three properties by hand for even a four element set already required examining eight pairs; this is exactly why, for any set beyond a handful of elements, verifying relation properties is done with code rather than manual inspection.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a relation must be defined by a formula; any arbitrary set of ordered pairs is a valid relation, formula or not.
Confusing the domain and range with the full sets A and B the relation was drawn from; elements that never appear in any pair are excluded from the domain or range even though they belong to A or B.
Assuming symmetry when only one direction of a connection has been observed, such as treating a directed follow relationship on a social network as if it were automatically mutual.
Assuming transitivity holds without checking every pair; a relation can look "chain-like" for a few examples and still fail transitivity somewhere else in the set.
Calling a relation an equivalence relation after checking only one or two of the three required properties, rather than confirming reflexive, symmetric, and transitive all hold.

blocks.text: These mistakes are especially easy to make when a relation is large or only partially inspected; always check reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity against the full set of pairs, or write a small verification function like the ones in this lesson, rather than eyeballing a handful of examples.

A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}

blocks.text: Before writing the grouping logic, it can help to first confirm the relation is symmetric and transitive by testing a handful of specific pairs by hand, since a bug in either check will silently produce equivalence classes that overlap or miss elements entirely.
Key Takeaway

A relation is nothing more than a set of ordered pairs connecting elements of two sets, or elements of one set to each other, and the three core properties, reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, describe exactly what kind of connection it represents. When all three hold together, the relation is an equivalence relation, and it automatically splits its underlying set into clean, non-overlapping equivalence classes.

Representing relations as matrices or directed graphs makes these properties visible at a glance, and that same graph representation is the direct bridge into the next lesson, graph theory basics, where vertices and edges become the primary object of study. Meanwhile, database joins and recommendation system user-item interactions are simply relations at industrial scale, which is exactly why the properties covered here, not just the notation, matter for building and reasoning about real systems.
